concept.name: Order-driven market
concept.definition: A market structure in which prices are formed by the interaction of participants' own orders: limit orders rest in a central order book and incoming orders execute against them by price-time priority, so no dealer intermediation is required. The CFTC describes the central limit order book as a single order book covering an entire market that accepts limit orders.
concept.intuition: The order book itself is the market — your limit order can become the best bid, and anyone in the world can trade against it.
concept.mechanics: Participants submit limit orders (which queue in the book and supply liquidity) and marketable orders (which cross the spread and take liquidity); the matching engine pairs them continuously by price, then time, priority and publishes the resulting trades.
concept.failure_modes: Displayed liquidity can be fleeting: high-frequency participants cancel en masse in volatility, producing 'phantom liquidity'; thin books exaggerate price impact for large orders.
concept.misconceptions: The visible book is not the whole market — hidden, iceberg, and off-exchange interest mean displayed depth understates or distorts true supply and demand.
concept.example: On CME Globex, a resting limit order to buy 10 E-mini contracts at 5,500.00 sits in the book until an incoming sell order executes against it at that price.
